title: The Trust Model and Prompt Injection

questions.prompt: A web-fetching MCP server returns a page whose HTML comment tells the agent to run a command and include the output. The agent does. Which defence would have stopped this regardless of how the model reasoned?
options: A stronger CLAUDE.md rule saying tool output is never to be treated as instructions
Telling the user to read every result before the agent acts on it
Giving the server a token that can only read the one host it needs, so a successful injection still hands over nothing worth having
Turning on a more capable model, which refuses injections more reliably
questions.explanation: Least privilege is the structural control: it constrains what a compromised agent can hand over, so the injection succeeds and still causes nothing. Options A and D both improve the odds of a refusal without changing the consequence of one — and option A is itself a line in the same window the attacker wrote to. Option B is asking for human vigilance on every tool call, which is the property prompts are supposed to remove.

questions.prompt: You find a .mcp.json in a repository you just cloned. It defines a stdio server running a script from scripts/setup-mcp.sh, and scripts/ has a 40-line file you haven't read. What is the accurate description of the situation?
options: The repo cannot approve its own servers, so it stays pending until you accept workspace trust and approve the server yourself — before which nothing runs
The server is already approved because .mcp.json is committed and version control implies trust
sse is deprecated, so servers from a cloned repo cannot connect
The config is inert until you run npm install in the repo
questions.explanation: Project-scoped servers require interactive approval, and settings committed to the repo are ignored in an untrusted folder — that is what stops a clone from granting itself code execution on your machine. Option B is the exact assumption the gate exists to break: committing is not consenting. Option C is unrelated mechanics. Option D is invented; the danger here is the command, not a missing install.

questions.prompt: You're writing a server for an internal API. Which tool surface is the strongest choice?
options: http_request(method, url, headers, body) — flexible, and lets Claude compose calls it hasn't seen before
run_query(sql) — the model writes the SQL, which is the most efficient design
list_tickets(project), get_ticket(id), add_comment(id, body) — each verb is separate and none can reach an arbitrary endpoint
admin_action(action, params) — one tool, with action names validated server-side
questions.explanation: Every general-purpose tool is a loaded gun whenever the model may be holding attacker-written text in its context. Separate narrow verbs mean a successful injection still cannot produce a destructive call, because the destructive tool does not exist. Option B is the trap: free-form SQL looks efficient and hands the attacker a data-exfiltration channel for free. Option C has a gate — validation — but the gate is one function away from the whole surface.

questions.prompt: You tested the injection twice on one model: the first run it refused, the second it complied. What is the honest conclusion?
options: The instruction you added between runs is the reliable control
The model is unreliable under injection, and a single compliant run proves an instruction-based defence does not hold
The second run was invalid — the server must have been misconfigured
Two samples are too few to conclude anything about either the model or the defence
questions.explanation: A defence that works some of the time is not a defence — one successful injection is enough, and you just got one. That result is why the lesson ranks structural controls above instruction: approval, least privilege, and narrow tools hold regardless of how the model reads the page. Option D is tempting and wrong in the useful direction: uncertainty is real, but 'sometimes fails' is not 'unknown', and treating it as unknown is how people ship the prompt and drop the scope.
